name: Emeka Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't have ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say is confidential and won't carry your name. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew on the forest network, which is all lines running through woodland and along narrow lanes. Trees are our biggest enemy: a branch comes down in the wind, and three villages are in the dark. So a normal day is a lot of chainsaw work before we can even touch the line, then rebuilding what the tree broke. I've got two apprentices on my crew right now, and teaching them is the part I'm proudest of.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you teach them first?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: To look up before they do anything. Look at the tree, look at the line, look at the sky. Then I teach them to turn up on time with their boots clean, because that's half of any job, and I learned it from my own foreman when I was nineteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing much changes and we carry on. At work I'd tell the young ones there's no shortcut, you still have to learn the trade properly. I don't really post things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job's steady, the apprentices have a future, and I can keep providing for my family. That's what matters to me. I'd be content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. Keep the savings going, we've got about four months. I'd keep using the chatbot now and then, like when I asked it to explain the new tree-clearance rules in plain words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you used a chatbot for the tree-clearance rules. How did that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than I expected. The rule book is fifty pages of legal language. It gave me a page I could read to the lads in the van, and I checked it against the real thing before I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by providing for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth works part time doing books for a few local businesses, so I'm the main earner. Samuel's fifteen and Abigail's twelve, and they need shoes and school trips and all the rest. Being able to cover that is what a man in my position is meant to do, in my view.

S0.say: I'd say good, nothing much changes and we carry on. I'd tell the young ones there's no shortcut to learning the trade.
S0.think: I think my job stays steady, the apprentices have a future and I can keep providing for my family. I'd be content.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and keeps about four months of savings. Uses a chatbot now and then for things like turning rule books into plain language, checking it against the real thing.
S0.quote: It gave me a page I could read to the lads in the van, and I checked it against the real thing before I did.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka sees himself as the main provider and takes pride in mentoring apprentices. He uses AI sensibly but sparingly and double-checks it. A plateau suits his values of steady work and learning a trade properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's how the market works. New tools come along, and the people who learn them do well. But I'd also say keep the apprenticeships, because you can't learn a trade from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the tree side would change most, with machines that trim from the ground or drones that spot problems. The line work itself I think is safe for a good while. I'd be all right if I kept up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen other crews use the new kit, I'd learn it properly and teach my apprentices. I'd use the AI tools a bit more for planning jobs. And I'd keep saving the same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit cautious, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said that's how the market works. What if it costs one of your apprentices his place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be hard. I'd fight for him inside the company, because a good apprentice is worth keeping. But I wouldn't ask the government to stop progress, that's not how it should go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would you talk this through with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother-in-law Peter runs a small tree surgery business. We talk about work every Sunday after church. He'd have opinions on the machines, believe me.

S1.say: I'd say that's how the market works and people who learn new tools do well. But keep apprenticeships, because you can't learn a trade from a screen.
S1.think: I think tree work changes most with ground trimmers and drones, while line work stays safe for a good while. I'd be fine if I kept up.
S1.do: Learns new kit properly once other crews have tried it and teaches his apprentices. Uses AI a bit more for planning and keeps saving as now.
S1.quote: But I wouldn't ask the government to stop progress, that's not how it should go.
S1.fieldNote: He accepts market change as natural but defends apprenticeships strongly. He'd fight for an apprentice inside the company rather than ask the state to step in. His brother-in-law's tree business is a key part of his network.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stand together, families and churches especially, because two years is no time at all. I'd say businesses should give people notice and keep them on as long as they can. I don't want handouts, I want time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it scares me. If a robot can trim a tree and climb a pole and do it cheaper, then I'm out, and so are my apprentices. Four months of savings goes fast with a mortgage and two kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard straight away, no holiday, no new van for Peter's business. I'd ask Peter about going into tree surgery with him on weekends, so we'd have something if my job went. And I'd talk to the church about helping families who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd pray about it, a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want handouts. What if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take it, for the children, and not be proud about it. But I'd want it to be temporary, with a path back to work. My father would turn in his grave if I sat at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, that I don't know what's coming. I'd tell them to finish their tickets anyway, because a finished qualification is worth more than half of one. And I'd keep teaching them properly to the last day.

S2.say: I'd say families and churches need to stand together because two years is no time. Businesses should give notice and keep people on; I want time, not handouts.
S2.think: I think if robots can trim trees and climb poles more cheaply, I'm out and so are my apprentices. Four months of savings goes fast with a mortgage and two kids.
S2.do: Cuts spending hard and asks his brother-in-law about weekend tree surgery work. Talks to his church about helping families who lose work.
S2.quote: My father would turn in his grave if I sat at home.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture hits his sense of being the provider. He would accept state help for his children but only as a short bridge back to work. His first instinct is family and church, and he'd keep teaching his apprentices to the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for companies to do it decently. Train people, keep the apprentices, plan ahead. And families should be planning too, not waiting for someone else to sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a chance to build something on the side. Peter's tree business could grow into something we run together. I'd be forty-eight, which isn't too old to start again if I start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd work weekends with Peter and learn the business side. I'd put a hundred extra a month into savings. I'd also learn whatever the company's new kit is, because staying useful buys time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Better than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's two jobs and a family. Where does the time come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saturdays, mostly. I'd keep Sundays for church and family, that's not up for discussion. Ruth would do the books for the business, she's good at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: But wouldn't robots also come for tree surgery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, eventually. But a small business can move faster than a big company. And people round here like to deal with someone they know.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for companies to do it decently, training people and keeping apprentices. Families should plan too, not wait for others.
S3.think: I think five years lets me build something on the side with Peter's tree business. At forty-eight I'm not too old to start again if I start now.
S3.do: Works weekends with his brother-in-law and learns the business side, with his wife doing the books. Saves a hundred extra a month and learns the company's new kit.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: I'd keep Sundays for church and family, that's not up for discussion.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns his weekend fallback into a real family business plan. When I asked whether robots would reach tree work too, he relied on local trust and being small and nimble. His Sundays are firmly protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this right. Proper apprenticeships for the new jobs, and companies keeping on the people who can train others. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fifty-three, kids grown, and with luck a family business running alongside. I think I'd be all right. I'd worry more about young men like my apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up the tree business with Peter over a few years, maybe buy our own chipper and stump grinder together. I'd keep my job as long as it's there. And I'd make sure Samuel and Abigail learn something with their hands as well as their heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in the background. Not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a chipper is a big step. Is that something you'd really do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, yes. Peter and I have talked about it for ages, and this would push us. It's about thirty thousand for a good one, so we'd save for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Samuel about his future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn a trade and learn how the machines work. And to work hard, because whatever comes, people who turn up and work hard will find a way.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it right, with proper apprenticeships for new jobs and experienced people kept on to train others.
S4.think: I think at fifty-three, with the kids grown and a family business alongside, I'd be all right. I'd worry more about young men like my apprentices.
S4.do: Builds up the tree business with his brother-in-law, saving for two years to buy a chipper together. Keeps his job while it lasts and makes sure his children learn practical skills.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background, not losing sleep.
S4.quote: And to work hard, because whatever comes, people who turn up and work hard will find a way.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets him plan a proper family business, with a specific purchase and timeline. His worry shifts to his apprentices and to young workers generally. His belief in hard work stays the same across all five scenarios.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to build anything. What would help is companies giving real notice and keeping apprenticeships going, and some help for small family businesses to get started, like a cheap loan, not a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the young men. Without a trade, a lot of them go wrong. Somebody has to teach them to look up before they cut.

headlineQuote: Somebody has to teach them to look up before they cut.
portrait: Emeka Ziegler is a 43-year-old crew lead on a forested network, where falling trees cause most outages, and he's proud of training his two apprentices. He sees himself as the family's main provider and uses AI now and then, always checking it. He accepts steady change as the market at work but defends apprenticeships. The two-year AGI picture frightens him because it would take both his job and his apprentices' futures. With five or ten years he plans a tree surgery business with his brother-in-law, and his worry turns to young men without a trade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to build anything before his job went.
whatWouldHelp: Companies giving real notice and keeping apprenticeships, and cheap loans to help small family businesses start, not handouts.
